t.3.58.2: Observing inauspicious omens again and again, he exclaimed, "Is all well with Sītā?"
t.3.58.1: As he was hurrying back, his lower left eye throbbed; Rāma stumbled, and a trembling came over him.
t.3.58.3: Then he went on in haste, eager to see Sītā, and seeing the dwelling empty, he became troubled in mind.
t.3.58.4: Raghunandana, as if whirling about in his haste and flinging out his arms, looked all around at the site of the hermitage here and there.
t.3.58.5: Then he saw the leaf-hut, empty of Sītā, bereft of its splendour and desolate, like a lotus pond ravaged in the winter season.
t.3.58.6: He saw it as if weeping through its trees, its flowers withered and its beasts and birds downcast, bereft of its splendor, ruined, and abandoned by the deities of the forest.
t.3.58.7: Seeing the empty site of the hut, its deerskins and kuśa grass scattered about and its mats and seats of woven grass tossed aside, he lamented again and again.
t.3.58.8: She must have been carried off, or she is dead, or lost, or devoured; or else the timid one has hidden herself, or has gone into the forest.
t.3.58.10: Though searching for her with great effort, he did not find his beloved in the forest; his eyes red with grief, he appeared as if maddened by sorrow.
t.3.58.9: Gone to gather flowers, or perhaps fruits as well? Or has she gone to a lotus pond, or gone to the river for water?
t.3.58.12: O Kadamba, have you perhaps seen my beloved, she who was fond of the kadamba tree? If you know of her, tell me of Sītā of the lovely face.
t.3.58.11: Running from tree to tree, over the mountains and from river to river, Rāma went on lamenting, sunk in an ocean of the mire of grief.
t.3.58.13: O bilva tree, tell me of her who resembles a tender, glossy shoot and is clad in yellow silk, if you have seen her, she whose breasts are like bilva fruits.
t.3.58.14: Or else, O Arjuna, tell me of that beloved one who was fond of arjuna trees: does the timid daughter of Janaka live or not?
t.3.58.15: The kakubha tree surely knows Maithilī, whose thighs are like the kakubha; for this lord of the forest shines, rich with creepers, tender shoots and flowers.
t.3.58.16: Since this excellent tree is serenaded by humming bees, this tilaka surely knows of her who is so fond of tilaka trees.
t.3.58.17: O Aśoka, dispeller of sorrow, my mind is stricken with grief; quickly make me worthy of your name, free of sorrow, by granting me the sight of my beloved.
t.3.58.18: O palm tree, if you have seen her whose breasts are like ripe palm fruits, tell me of that fair-hipped lady, if you have any compassion for me.
t.3.58.19: O Jambu tree, if you have seen Sītā, radiant as jāmbūnada gold, if you know of my beloved, tell me without hesitation.
t.3.58.20: Or perhaps, O deer, you know Maithilī, whose eyes are like a fawn's? My beloved, whose glances are like a deer's, may be with the does.
t.3.58.21: O elephant, if she whose thighs are like an elephant's trunk has been seen by you, I think she is known to you; tell me of her, O best of elephants.
t.3.58.22: O tiger, if you have seen my beloved Maithilī, whose face is like the moon, tell me without hesitation; you have nothing to fear.
t.3.58.23: Why do you run away, beloved? Surely you have been seen, O lotus-eyed one! Having hidden yourself behind a tree, why do you not answer me?
t.3.58.24: Stay, stay, O fair-hipped one! Have you no compassion for me? You are not one much given to jesting, so why do you disregard me?
t.3.58.25: You are betrayed by your yellow silk garment, O lady of fair complexion; even as you run away, I have seen you. Stop, if there is any affection for me in you!
t.3.58.27: Clearly that young girl, my beloved, separated from me, has been devoured by flesh-eating Rākṣasas, who tore all her limbs apart.
t.3.58.26: Surely she is no more, or else the sweetly smiling one has been harmed; for distress has indeed befallen me, and she would surely never disregard me like this.
t.3.58.28: Surely that face with its lovely teeth and lips has lost its radiance, and so too that neck, which shone with the hue of the campaka flower and was adorned with a necklace.
t.3.58.29: Surely, as my beloved lamented, her tender and lovely form was devoured, and those two arms of hers, soft as young shoots, must have been flung about.
t.3.58.30: Her two arms, trembling at their tips, have been devoured along with her hands, ornaments and armlets; separated from me, the young woman has surely become food for the Rākṣasas.
t.3.58.31: Like one abandoned by her caravan, she who had many kinsmen has been devoured. Alas, mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa, do you see my beloved anywhere?
t.3.58.33: Now he rushes up in haste, now he wanders about with force; at times, wholly intent on searching for his beloved, he appears like one gone mad.
t.3.58.32: "Alas, beloved, where have you gone, gentle lady? Alas, Sītā!" Crying out thus again and again, Rāma, lamenting in this way, ran about from forest to forest.
t.3.58.34: He wanders swiftly, never coming to rest, through woods, rivers and mountains, mountain springs and forests.
t.3.58.35: Thus he went into the vast and mighty forest and searched all of it for Maithilī; then, his hope not yet exhausted, he once more made the utmost effort in the search for his beloved.
